title: Ezekiel 20:10–26
context: The LORD continues the history through Ezekiel. He brought Israel into the wilderness, gave them statutes and ordinances by which a person who does them will live (compare Leviticus 18:5), and gave his Sabbaths as a sign that he sanctifies them (compare Exodus 31:13). The first generation rebelled, and the LORD swore they would not enter the land, yet he spared them for his name’s sake (compare Numbers 14:23, 29). He warned their children not to follow their fathers’ statutes, but they rebelled too, and he swore to scatter them among the nations (compare Psalm 106:26–27). Verse 25 says the LORD gave them statutes that were not good and ordinances in which they could not live, and verse 26 says he polluted them in their own gifts when they made all that opens the womb pass through the fire. This is a well-known difficulty, and interpreters read it in several ways. Many take it as judicial giving over, in which God handed the people over to the corrupt customs they had chosen (compare 20:39; Psalm 81:12; Acts 7:42; Romans 1:24). Others take the not good statutes to be the pagan statutes of the fathers that the children adopted (20:18). Some connect verse 26 with the law of the firstborn (Exodus 13:2; 22:29), which the people distorted into child sacrifice, a practice the law itself forbids (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 18:10; compare Jeremiah 7:31). Some read the line as ironic or rhetorical. Readers in both Arminian and Reformed traditions generally agree that the verse does not mean God commanded child sacrifice or is the author of sin. They describe God’s part in judgment somewhat differently, as they do at Judges 9:23 and Romans 1:24. No single reading has won general agreement.

verses.text: So I caused them to go out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD bringing Israel out of Egypt into the wilderness. Deliverance came despite their rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s mercy carrying the people forward. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the gracious pattern the chapter traces.

verses.text: I gave them my statutes and showed them my ordinances, which if a man does, he will live in them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD giving statutes and ordinances by which a person who does them will live. The law was given for life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the echo of Leviticus 18:5 and the goodness of God’s law. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as affirming that God’s commands were meant for Israel’s good.

verses.text: Moreover also I gave them my Sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD giving his Sabbaths as a sign that he sanctifies his people. Rest marked their relationship with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Sabbath as a covenant sign (compare Exodus 31:13). Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that holiness comes from the LORD who sanctifies.

verses.text: “ ‘ “But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They didn’t walk in my statutes and they rejected my ordinances, which if a man keeps, he shall live in them. They greatly profaned my Sabbaths. Then I said I would pour out my wrath on them in the wilderness, to consume them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel rebelling in the wilderness, rejecting God’s ordinances and profaning his Sabbaths. The LORD resolved to consume them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same rebellion repeated after deliverance. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober reminder of persistent human unfaithfulness.

verses.text: But I worked for my name’s sake, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I brought them out.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD again acting for his name’s sake rather than destroying the people. Mercy prevails for the sake of his reputation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s name as the steady ground of his patience. Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to his purpose.

verses.text: Moreover also I swore to them in the wilderness that I would not bring them into the land which I had given them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD swearing that the rebellious generation would not enter the land. Their choices had real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath recalled from Numbers 14:23. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s mercy does not cancel his justice.

verses.text: because they rejected my ordinances, and didn’t walk in my statutes, and profaned my Sabbaths; for their heart went after their idols.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the reason: they rejected God’s ordinances and their hearts went after idols. Idolatry begins in the heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heart’s inclination toward idols as the root of disobedience. Both traditions commonly read the verse as diagnosing sin at its source.

verses.text: Nevertheless my eye spared them, and I didn’t destroy them. I didn’t make a full end of them in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD sparing the people and not making a full end of them in the wilderness. Even in judgment, compassion remained.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s preserving mercy toward his people. Readers in both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s patience with the rebellious.

verses.text: I said to their children in the wilderness, ‘Don’t walk in the statutes of your fathers. Don’t observe their ordinances or defile yourselves with their idols.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD warning the children not to follow their fathers’ statutes and idols. Each generation is called to choose faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God calling the next generation away from inherited sin. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that the past need not determine the future.

verses.text: I am the LORD your God. Walk in my statutes, keep my ordinances, and do them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he is their God and calling them to walk in his statutes. The call is clear and personal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant claim, I am the LORD your God, grounding the command. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about obedience flowing from relationship.

verses.text: Make my Sabbaths holy. They shall be a sign between me and you, that you may know that I am the LORD your God.’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the call to make the Sabbaths holy as a sign that they may know the LORD. Rest and worship belong together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Sabbath as a sign of covenant knowledge of God. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of God’s gracious instruction to the second generation.

verses.text: “ ‘ “But the children rebelled against me. They didn’t walk in my statutes, and didn’t keep my ordinances to do them, which if a man does, he shall live in them. They profaned my Sabbaths. Then I said I would pour out my wrath on them, to accomplish my anger against them in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the children also rebelling, refusing the statutes by which one lives, and profaning the Sabbaths. The pattern repeats.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see sin passed from generation to generation. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober account of covenant failure.

verses.text: Nevertheless I withdrew my hand and worked for my name’s sake, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I brought them out.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD withdrawing his hand and acting for his name’s sake. God’s restraint is a gift the people did not deserve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s glory again staying his hand. Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s purpose standing behind his mercy.

verses.text: Moreover I swore to them in the wilderness, that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the countries,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD swearing in the wilderness that he would scatter them among the nations. Exile was foreseen as a consequence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s warning of exile already present in the wilderness (compare Psalm 106:27). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse in light of the covenant warnings.

verses.text: because they had not executed my ordinances, but had rejected my statutes, and had profaned my Sabbaths, and their eyes were after their fathers’ idols.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the reason given: they rejected God’s statutes and looked after their fathers’ idols. Their own choices brought judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the justice of God’s dealings with a persistently idolatrous people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as connecting judgment to real sin.

verses.text: Moreover also I gave them statutes that were not good, and ordinances in which they couldn’t live.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers commonly read the statutes that were not good as God giving the people over to the corrupt customs they chose, a judgment that follows persistent rebellion (compare Psalm 81:12). Other readings are also held.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly read the line as a judicial act in which God hands sinners over to their own ways (compare Romans 1:24), while denying that God is the author of sin. Readers in both traditions hold the crux with care.

verses.text: I polluted them in their own gifts, in that they caused all that opens the womb to pass through the fire, that I might make them desolate, to the end that they might know that I am the LORD.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he polluted them in their gifts when they passed the firstborn through the fire. They see a judgment that let a forbidden practice reveal their ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same judgment and note that the law itself forbade such offerings (compare Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 18:10). Both traditions commonly agree God never commanded child sacrifice.
